finding.claim: isInSubnet/isHostInSubnet compare raw leading bits across address families, so an Address6 holding an IPv4-mapped address (::ffff:10.0.0.1) never matches an Address4 CIDR (10.0.0.0/8). An allow/deny check written with the IPv4 range returns false for the mapped form.
finding.source: Attacker-chosen host literal parsed by new Address6(input), e.g. '::ffff:10.0.0.1' from a URL or user field. Precondition: consumer calls addr.isInSubnet(new Address4('10.0.0.0/8')) (the signature accepts Address4|Address6 and nothing warns against it).
finding.sink: Trust-boundary decision (SSRF deny/allow) on the result of isInSubnet/isHostInSubnet.

trace.note: isInSubnet: subnetMask check 128 < 8 is false, so falls through to host compare
isHostInSubnet: this.mask(address.subnetMask) === address.mask(), i.e. this.mask(8)='00000000' vs Address4 10.x -> '00001010'

finding.guards_checked: Checked subnet-length guard (common.ts:20) and host-bit comparison; no family-type check exists anywhere in common.ts. Same-family calls (Address6 vs Address6) are correct. The embeddedIPv4()-based isPrivate()/isLoopback() on Address6 (ipv6.ts:1375) does handle mapped addresses, so the bug only affects callers who use the CIDR-style isInSubnet with an Address4 range.

finding.claim: simpleGroup returns any group token containing 'group-v4' without HTML escaping, so the exported helper passes raw attacker markup through when given untrusted text.
finding.source: Caller-supplied string passed to the public helper v6.helpers.simpleGroup(input). Precondition: consumer exposes that helper to untrusted input and renders the result as HTML.
finding.sink: Returned HTML fragment inserted into innerHTML/markup by the consumer.

trace.note: helpers module exported publicly as v6.helpers (ip-address.ts:7)
Non-matching groups go through spanLeadingZeroesSimple -> escapeHtml, so only the group-v4 branch is unescaped

finding.guards_checked: escapeHtml is applied on the other branch (helpers.ts:32, 56). Address6.group() (ipv6.ts:1509-1551) is not reachable with this input because the constructor rejects any non-hex/colon character (ipv6.ts:801-810), so the bypass needs direct use of the exported helper. Other exported helpers (spanAll, spanLeadingZeroes, link, parse4in6 prefix) escape correctly.

finding.claim: RE_ZONE_STRING = /%.*$/ is quadratic on input containing many '%' followed by a line terminator, because '.' does not match \n/\r/ /  and '$' is not multiline. Each '%' start scans to the terminator and backtracks. This runs before the bad-character check, so the cost hits every constructor call.
finding.source: Attacker-controlled string passed to new Address6(s) or Address6.isValid(s), e.g. a JSON body field (JSON can carry \n; HTTP headers cannot). Example: '%'.repeat(N) + '\n'.
finding.sink: Synchronous RegExp.exec on the event loop (CPU exhaustion / event-loop block). Estimated about N^2/2 backtrack steps; not executed.

trace.note: parse() runs only afterwards, so bad-character rejection is too late to help

finding.guards_checked: Checked Node header limits (no raw newlines in headers) and the anchors: the regex has $ but no m flag, so it fails at the terminator instead of matching early. Subnet regex and RE_URL/RE_URL_WITH_PORT are linear. Only the zone regex is affected. Not verified by execution (no shell available in this session).

finding.claim: href() interpolates optionalPort into the URL with no validation, so a string port containing '@' or '/' changes the URL authority/host (e.g. href('1@evil.example') -> http://[::1]:1@evil.example/).
finding.source: Consumer passes untrusted string as the port argument (typed number|string). Precondition: consumer builds a fetch/redirect URL from href() with user-supplied port.
finding.sink: URL string returned to the consumer for a request or link (host confusion / SSRF / open redirect).

trace.note: optionalPort = `:${optionalPort}` with no type or digit check

finding.guards_checked: Host part is validated (correctForm of a validated address, so no brackets/@ in it). Port is not validated anywhere. Attack requires a consumer to pass untrusted data as the port.

finding.claim: AddressError.parseMessage for bad characters contains raw, unescaped input, contrary to the documented contract that it is HTML-escaped and safe to insert as-is.
finding.source: Attacker-controlled address string, e.g. '">'.
finding.sink: Consumer inserting err.parseMessage as HTML (per the documented contract).

trace.note: address.replace(RE_BAD_CHARACTERS, '$1') with no escapeHtml; the matched char is inserted raw
doc claims 'The address content is HTML-escaped, so it is safe to insert as-is'

finding.guards_checked: In text context the wrapper keeps every raw '<' followed by '', so no tag can form and no text-context XSS was found. Raw '"' and "'" survive, so the claim fails inside quoted attributes. Bad-address branch (ipv6.ts:817) is safe (only hex/:/% reach it). parse4in6 prefix (ipv6.ts:763) is escaped. Low severity: exploitable only if a consumer uses the documented HTML in an attribute context.

finding.claim: testBit reads bit position-1 instead of position (index length-p should be length-1-p), so Teredo flags coneNat, reserved, universalLocal and groupIndividual are wrong. For example, a cone-NAT flag of 1 is reported as false.
finding.source: Attacker-controlled IPv6 address in 2001::/32 passed to inspectTeredo().
finding.sink: Decoded Teredo metadata returned to the caller (informational; no decision in this library uses it).

trace.note: positionInString = length - position = 1 for position 15, so reads index 1 (bit 14, the reserved bit)
groupIndividual = testBit(flagsBase2, 8) reads the A bit at index 8; universalLocal = testBit(9) reads the G bit

finding.guards_checked: Checked the other Teredo fields (server4, client4, udpPort XOR, nonce slicing), which match RFC 4380 layout. Only the flag booleans are wrong. Impact is incorrect data, not a security bypass, within this library.
